support: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective. A bigger image is not always a clearer image. Describe what you can see before you explain it.

video.title: Microscopy
video.question: What is the difference between making an image bigger and resolving more detail?

extra.say: Magnification is how many times larger an image is. Resolution is whether close points can be seen separately. Enlarging a blur does not recover detail.
extra.trap: Do not add the lens powers. At high power use fine focus only; follow the microscope’s approved procedure.

activity.title: Lens detective
activity.prompt: Choose the first safe step. Then predict what changes at higher power.
activity.check: With a ×10 eyepiece: ×4 gives ×40; ×40 gives ×400. The field of view shrinks. A larger image is not automatically clearer.

support: 1. Name the missing value. 2. Match the units. 3. Choose M = I ÷ A, I = M × A or A = I ÷ M. 4. Show each line of working.

video.title: Microscopy
video.question: What is the difference between making an image bigger and resolving more detail?

extra.say: Name the unknown, match the units, select the relationship, substitute, then check. Magnification is a ratio: write ×200, not 200 mm.
extra.trap: 50 µm is 0.05 mm, not 50 mm. A correct final value is not evidence that the unit route was understood.

activity.title: Choose the relationship
activity.prompt: Work in pairs: one chooses the formula; one checks the units. Swap.
items: A   Image 20 mm; actual 0.1 mm. Find M.
B   Image 50 mm; actual 0.5 mm. Find M.
C   M = ×400; actual 0.05 mm. Find image size.
activity.check:
A: 20 ÷ 0.1 = ×200.
B: 50 ÷ 0.5 = ×100.
C: 400 × 0.05 = 20 mm.
Keep units for lengths; magnification is a ratio.

support: Check the units first. Then check the calculation. For a scale bar, count how many bar lengths fit the cell image.

video.title: Microscopy
video.question: What is the difference between making an image bigger and resolving more detail?

extra.say: A ruler measurement changes if a picture is resized. A scale bar stays useful if the image and bar are resized together.
extra.trap: Do not claim pupils measured a real cell if they used stated lengths or a model. A precise-looking number is not automatically an accurate measurement.

activity.title: Find the first faulty step
activity.prompt: Image length = 32 mm. Actual length = 80 µm.
items: Repair it, keeping the first attempt visible.
activity.check:
The units do not match.
32 mm = 32,000 µm.
M = 32,000 ÷ 80 = ×400.
Check units before arithmetic.

topic: Diffusion: Net Movement Down a Gradient
support: Net movement = crossings one way minus crossings the other way. Start: “More particles move from ___ to ___ because…”

video.title: Diffusion
video.question: What keeps happening when there is no net movement?

extra.say: Particles move randomly in both directions. Net movement is the difference between those two movements, not a rule obeyed by every particle.
extra.trap: Passive means no energy supplied by respiration is needed. It does not mean particles have no kinetic energy.

activity.title: Count both directions
activity.prompt: Equal volumes: 12 particles on the left, 3 on the right. Predict the initial net direction.
activity.after: Find the net crossing count for each interval. What keeps happening at balance?
activity.check:
Early: 8 − 2 = 6 net left to right.
At balance: 5 − 5 = 0 net.
Particles still move randomly and cross both ways. These are illustrative model counts.

support: Use three parts: the feature, what it changes, and how that affects diffusion. Start: “Thin walls help because…”

video.title: Gas exchange in the lungs
video.question: How does a thin wall help oxygen move into the blood?

extra.say: For each feature, say what it changes physically and why that affects diffusion. “Good lungs” is not an explanation.
extra.trap: Both alveolar and capillary walls contribute to the diffusion path. Do not describe oxygen as choosing a destination.

activity.title: Build a linked explanation
activity.prompt: Point to the net direction for each gas. Then explain one adaptation.
table: Alveolar air compared with arriving blood
activity.after: Thin walls → what physical effect? → how does this help diffusion?
activity.check:
Oxygen: air → blood. Carbon dioxide: blood → air.
Thin walls give a short diffusion distance, so gases cross more quickly down their gradients. Blood flow and ventilation help maintain gradients.

support: Describe: what changes in the numbers? Explain: why does it change? Start: “When the area doubles, ___ because…”

video.title: Diffusion
video.question: What keeps happening when there is no net movement?

extra.say: Describe tells us the pattern. Explain links that pattern to a mechanism. Evaluation asks whether the evidence supports the conclusion.
extra.trap: Dye spreading in warm water can include convection. Do not present an uncontrolled demonstration as proof of diffusion rate alone.

activity.title: Hold an evidence conference
activity.prompt: Concentration difference, membrane and temperature are unchanged.
activity.after: Choose a pattern, explain it, then name one limit of this model.
activity.check: Area doubles, and transfer doubles in these model data. More surface allows more particles to cross at once. This does not establish real medicine doses or biological effects.

support: Name the substance that moves. Check which solution is more dilute. Add the membrane and net direction. Start: “Water moves…”

video.title: Osmosis
video.question: Which substance moves, through what, and in which net direction?

extra.say: Osmosis is net water movement through a partially permeable membrane from a more dilute to a more concentrated solution.
extra.trap: The potato is tissue, not a single membrane. Its cells have membranes. “Concentrated” must be relative to the solution on the other side.

activity.title: Make a membrane decision
activity.prompt: Predict net water movement. State which solution you are comparing with the cell solution.
activity.check:
A: net water movement into the cell.
B: no net movement; water still moves both ways.
C: net water movement out of the cell.
Osmosis needs a partially permeable membrane.

support: Change = final mass minus initial mass. Percentage change = change ÷ initial mass × 100. Keep the + or - sign.

video.title: Osmosis
video.question: Which substance moves, through what, and in which net direction?

extra.say: Today’s default cover route is planning and sample-data analysis. A full soak, repeated measurements and graph do not fit inside a six-minute shared-task slot.
extra.trap: Only record practical completion for pupils who actually carry out the approved practical. Sample data and pre-soaked staff samples are not proof of that completion.

activity.title: Plan a fair comparison
activity.prompt: Sample data. Calculate signed change, then choose a control.
activity.after: What should stay the same? What would inconsistent blotting do?
activity.check:
Water: +0.40 g, +10%.
0.4 mol dm⁻³: 0 g, 0%.
0.8 mol dm⁻³: −0.40 g, −10%.
Standardise blotting: surface liquid changes the measured final mass.

support: Find each mean: add the repeats and divide by their number. Describe the trend. Keep unusual results visible and explain any choice to leave one out.

video.title: Osmosis
video.question: Which substance moves, through what, and in which net direction?

extra.say: Keep the raw data visible. Flag unusual values and investigate. Never delete a value simply because the graph looks tidier without it.
extra.trap: Between +12% at 0.2 and −8% at 0.6, straight-line interpolation gives 0.44 mol dm⁻³, not the midpoint 0.4.

activity.title: Keep the unusual result
activity.prompt: Illustrative samples. Calculate the means; estimate where change is zero.
activity.after: An extra repeat at 0.6 gives +9%. What should happen before excluding it?
activity.check:
Means: +20, +12, +2, −8, −20%.
Nearest crossing: 0.4 + (2 ÷ 10) × 0.2 ≈ 0.44 mol dm⁻³.
Retain and flag +9%; check the record and method before deciding. With it, the 0.6 mean is −3.75%.

support: Compare the concentration outside and inside. Add an inward arrow. Start: “The ions move from ___ to ___. This needs…”

video.title: Active transport
video.question: What two clues distinguish active transport from diffusion?

extra.say: Active transport uses energy released by respiration to move a substance against its concentration gradient through membrane transport proteins.
extra.trap: Diffusion is random at particle level. The contrast is net movement down a gradient versus energy-dependent movement against it, not “diffusion never moves backwards”.

activity.title: Predict the energy effect
activity.prompt: Equal-volume regions: 2 nitrate ions outside, 8 inside. Net movement of nitrate ions is inwards.
items: Which way is movement relative to the gradient?
What does the membrane transport protein need?
Predict what happens if respiration is reduced.
activity.check: Inward movement is lower → higher: against the gradient. Active transport needs energy released by respiration. Less available energy reduces uptake. An instant on/off model simplifies a real cell.

support: Use two clues: direction compared with the gradient, and what happens when respiration is reduced. Start: “This suggests ___ because…”

video.title: Active transport
video.question: What two clues distinguish active transport from diffusion?

extra.say: Use two clues: direction relative to the gradient and dependence on respiration. “Root hair” or “gut” alone does not determine every transport mechanism.
extra.trap: The gut can use more than one transport mechanism. Here the stated against-gradient uptake and energy evidence support active transport.

activity.title: Use two clues
activity.prompt: Model values use the same concentration units. Uptake is inwards.
activity.after: Use direction and energy evidence. Does the cell’s location alone prove the mechanism?
activity.check: Both movements are against the gradient; uptake falls when respiration is inhibited. Together these support active transport. Root hair or gut alone does not determine every transport mechanism.

support: Ask: what moves, which way compared with the gradient, and is cellular energy needed? If a clue is missing, say what more you need to know.

video.title: Active transport
video.question: What two clues distinguish active transport from diffusion?

extra.say: Read the evidence before naming the process. Some statements belong to more than one process; some scenarios do not contain enough information.
extra.trap: “Water only” points to osmosis, but the membrane and relative solutions still matter. Movement through a membrane alone does not prove active transport.

activity.title: Sort the transport clues
activity.prompt: Choose diffusion, osmosis, active transport or need more evidence. Give the deciding clue.
items: A   Oxygen moves from higher concentration in air into blood.
B   Water crosses a partially permeable membrane from a solution more dilute than the cell contents.
C   Ions enter against their gradient using energy from respiration.
D   A substance crosses a membrane. No other clue is given.
activity.check:
A: diffusion — down the oxygen gradient.
B: osmosis — water, membrane, dilute to concentrated.
C: active transport — against gradient using cellular energy.
D: insufficient evidence — ask what moves, which gradient and whether energy is needed.

support: Choose two ideas. Link them with “because” or “whereas”. For a cell adaptation, name the feature and what it helps the cell do.

video.title: Microscopy
video.question: What is the difference between making an image bigger and resolving more detail?

extra.say: This reviews cells, microscopy and transport taught so far. It is not a claim that every part of GCSE Topic 1, including enzymes, has been completed.
extra.trap: Do not turn confidence colours into public rankings. Ask for a piece of work or a corrected explanation to support a review choice.

activity.title: Repair the knowledge map
activity.prompt: Choose two ideas. Connect them using because or whereas. Your partner checks the science.
activity.check:
Matching units makes a magnification ratio valid.
Mass change can provide evidence of net water movement by osmosis.
Respiration releases energy for active transport.
Accept other accurate, explained links.

support: Describe = say what happens. Explain = say why. Compare = link a similarity or difference. Calculate = show working. Evaluate = judge using evidence.

video.title: Gas exchange in the lungs
video.question: How does a thin wall help oxygen move into the blood?

extra.say: The command word tells you the kind of answer. Marks depend on the question and its mark scheme, not magic words such as “whereas”.
extra.trap: “Evaluate” is more than listing improvements: weigh relevant evidence or method strengths/limits and make a supported judgement where asked.

activity.title: Run a command-word clinic
activity.prompt: Sample graph: sucrose 0.2 → 0.6 mol dm⁻³; mass change +12% → −8%. Improve each answer.
activity.check:
Describe a numerical pattern.
Explain: thin walls → short diffusion distance → faster exchange.
Evaluate: repeat each concentration to measure spread and calculate a mean; also standardise blotting. Repeats alone do not fix a systematic error.

support: Choose one real answer. Underline the part you will improve. Write the change in your own words and say why it is clearer.

activity.title: Rehearse the answer shape
activity.prompt: This is practice. Keep assessment Q2, Q3 and Q5 for your own first attempt.
items: Explain why thin alveolar walls help gas exchange.
Choose the cause and the consequence.
activity.check:
Explain needs a scientific cause linked to a consequence.
Thin walls give a short diffusion distance, so oxygen diffuses into blood more quickly down its gradient.
Now use your own reasoning for the independent questions.
